pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–10 years

- **Topic:** Levers, Pulleys & Gears

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, Year 5 Forces):** Recognise that some mechanisms including levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect (verbatim this topic); it ties forward to KS3 moments / mechanical advantage.

- **Standards — US (NGSS — no direct simple-machines PE at this grade band):** NGSS has no direct simple-machines performance expectation at the elementary band; the topic is UK-curriculum anchored and links forward to NGSS forces/energy and engineering-design ideas (e.g. MS-PS3, MS-ETS1) later.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A→B boundary (concrete/observational moving toward early-formal, age 9-10). The goal is the QUALITATIVE big idea — levers, pulleys and gears let a smaller force have a greater effect, with a lever's effort depending on where the pivot sits — grounded in measuring real effort, NOT the quantitative moment = force × distance (reserve for KS3, topic mt_vuNjYx3qOy).
bestPractices: Anchor in measurement: use force meters, a stiff ruler/rod, masses and a pivot so children MEASURE that the effort needed to lift a fixed load drops as the effort is applied further from (and the pivot is moved closer to) the load.
Name the three lever parts in child-friendly terms — load (object being lifted), effort (force you apply), pivot/fulcrum (fixed point it turns on) — teaching 'pivot' and 'fulcrum' together.
Teach honestly that a machine does not create force from nothing — it trades force for distance: less effort means moving the effort end a greater distance (keeps the big idea from becoming 'magic').

Cover all three mechanisms and what each changes: lever (reduce effort by pivot position), pulley (change the direction of the force, and adding wheels reduces effort), gears (change size and/or direction of force; small gear turns fast with less force, large gear slow with more).
Classify and connect to everyday objects — seesaw, crowbar, scissors, wheelbarrow, bottle opener, tweezers, the elbow joint — so the abstraction is grounded in things children know.
Use predict-then-measure: predict where to put the pivot for least effort, then test and read the force meter, so the relationship is evidenced not asserted.
keyRepresentations: A lever (ruler) on a movable pivot with a mass as load and a force meter reading the effort — slide the pivot, watch the effort change
Seesaw as the relatable first-class lever model (effort/load/pivot)
A pulley with a string and hanging load; add a wheel to see effort fall and/or direction change
Two meshed gears of different sizes (small fast/low force vs large slow/high force)
Everyday-object cards labelled with effort/load/pivot for classification
commonMisconceptions: 'All levers work the same way' (Oak) — children miss that pivot position and effort-vs-load placement change how much effort is needed.
Thinking a machine creates extra force from nothing — missing the force-for-distance trade-off.
'Gears only exist in bicycles and cars' (Oak) — not recognising gears more widely.
'All pulleys have the wheel fixed to a ceiling' (Oak) — over-narrow image of a pulley.
Confusing which part is the effort and which is the load, especially in second/third-class arrangements (wheelbarrow, tweezers).

learn.summary: For ages 9–10 (UK Year 5 Forces), teach the qualitative big idea that levers, pulleys and gears let a smaller force have a greater effect — and that this is not free, but a trade: you apply a smaller force but must move the effort end a greater distance. Anchor in real measurement (force meters, a rigid ruler/rod, masses, a movable pivot) using predict-then-measure, supported where helpful by an on-screen workbench that recomputes effort live as the pivot moves. Name load, effort and pivot/fulcrum, cover all three mechanisms and what each changes, and connect to everyday objects to challenge 'all levers work the same' and over-narrow images of pulleys and gears. Reserve quantitative moment = force × distance for later (KS3).

activities.title: Measure the effort drop on a real lever (predict-then-measure)
feedback: If a child predicts 'it makes no difference where the pivot is', have them measure both positions: the force-meter reading visibly changes, so pivot and effort position matter.

If a child says the lever 'lifts for free' or 'makes you stronger', ask what their end of the bar had to do — show the effort end moves much further than the load rises, so the smaller force is paid for by the greater distance moved; nothing is free.
Confirm correct reasoning: 'A smaller force lifts the load because the pivot is close to the load and the effort is far from it, and the cost is that your end moves a longer way.'
activities.rationale: Grounding the cause-effect relationship in real measurement with predict-then-measure lets the relationship be evidenced rather than asserted, and directly probes the 'all levers work the same' and 'lifts for free' misconceptions. Reading a real (noisy) force meter and feeling the effort drop is a sensory/measurement anchor central at this age.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: recognise that some mechanisms including levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect; non-statutory guidance suggests exploring their effects on movement and designing products using them.

A lever allows a smaller force to have a greater effect; load = object lifted, effort = force applied, pivot/fulcrum = fixed turning point; effort needed depends on where the pivot sits; gears change size/direction of force (small gear fast/less force, large gear slow/more force); misconception 'all levers work the same way'; equipment = force meters, rulers/rods, masses.

A lever (and any simple machine) trades force for distance — more force gives less distance and vice versa; positioning the fulcrum close to a heavy load lets a small effort lift it; build-and-test with a ruler and pencil pivot to observe how fulcrum position changes effort.
learnerActions: Set up a stiff ruler or rod across a movable pivot (e.g. a pencil or small log), with a fixed mass as the load near one end.
Before testing, predict: as you move the pivot toward the load (and apply the effort further from the pivot), will the effort needed go up or down — and why? Write or say your prediction.
Hook a force meter at the effort end (or push and feel the effort) and read the effort needed to lift the fixed load with the pivot in its first position.
Slide the pivot closer to the load, repeat the measurement, and record how the force-meter reading changes.
Notice and describe what your hand/the effort end has to do: how far it moves compared with how far the load rises.
activities.intendedInsight: As the pivot moves closer to the load, so that the effort is applied further from the pivot than the load is, the effort needed to lift a fixed load drops. A smaller force has a greater effect, but the effort end travels a longer distance. You apply a smaller force at the cost of moving further. The lever does not create energy: the bigger force on the load is paid for by your end moving further.

activities.title: On-screen mechanism workbench: drag the pivot and watch effort change
feedback: If the child expects the effort to stay the same when dragging the pivot, pause on the falling needle and ask them to relate it to where the pivot now sits.
If the child treats the longer arc as unimportant, link it explicitly: the meter shows less force, the arc shows more distance — that is the trade.

For pulley mode, prompt: did adding the wheel change how hard you pull, the direction you pull, or both? Remind them a fixed overhead wheel only changes direction, while a movable wheel lowers the effort.
For gear mode, prompt: the small gear turns fast with less turning force; the large gear turns slowly with more turning force — which did you drive and which did it turn?
activities.rationale: A relationship between pivot position and effort suits an interactive that recomputes a force-meter live and renders the force-for-distance trade as a longer arc. This is proposed as a strong digital model that makes the mechanism legible in a 2D cross-section; it should accompany, not replace, real measurement.
sourceClaims: Year 5 statutory: recognise that some mechanisms including levers, pulleys and gears allow a smaller force to have a greater effect; non-statutory guidance suggests exploring their effects on movement and designing products using them.

A lever allows a smaller force to have a greater effect; load = object lifted, effort = force applied, pivot/fulcrum = fixed turning point; effort needed depends on where the pivot sits; gears change size/direction of force (small gear fast/less force, large gear slow/more force); misconception 'all levers work the same way'; equipment = force meters, rulers/rods, masses.
learnerActions: On a lever workbench, try to lift a heavy crate; read the force-meter with the pivot in the middle — the reading is high because, with equal distances either side of the pivot, the push needed is about the same as the load's weight (it needs a big push).
Predict what will happen to the effort, then drag the pivot toward the crate and watch the effort reading fall as the same load lifts under a gentler push.
Observe the ghosted 'effort arc' showing the effort end sweeping through a longer path — name the bargain: less force, more distance.

Switch to pulley mode: thread an extra movable (supporting) wheel to build toward a block-and-tackle and watch the effort reading fall; note that a single fixed wheel would only change the direction you pull, while a movable wheel reduces the effort.
Switch to gear mode: mesh a small driver gear into a large gear and describe what happens to force and to speed/direction.
activities.intendedInsight: The live recompute of the effort meter as the pivot/pulley/gears change makes 'a smaller force has a greater effect' something the child drives and sees, including the force-for-distance trade shown as a longer effort arc. A fixed pulley changes direction; a movable pulley reduces effort.

activities.title: Name the parts and classify everyday machines
feedback: If a child swaps effort and load on a wheelbarrow or tweezers, have them identify what is being lifted (load) versus where they apply force (effort), then find the fixed pivot.
If a child says gears are only in bikes and cars, show an egg-whisk or clock; if they think a pulley only hangs from a ceiling, show a movable pulley that reduces effort.

Reinforce: on a lever like the ruler or seesaw, where the pivot is between the load and the effort and you push at the far end, moving the pivot toward the load reduces the effort needed. This matches what the measurement and workbench showed. Remember that some levers, like tweezers, need more effort instead.
activities.rationale: Classifying and labelling gives targeted consolidation and directly probes the 'all levers work the same' and over-narrow pulley/gear images; this task can check and reinforce classification and vocabulary but does not itself produce the measured relationship or the felt effort drop, so it best follows hands-on measurement.
sourceClaims: A lever allows a smaller force to have a greater effect; load = object lifted, effort = force applied, pivot/fulcrum = fixed turning point; effort needed depends on where the pivot sits; gears change size/direction of force (small gear fast/less force, large gear slow/more force); misconception 'all levers work the same way'; equipment = force meters, rulers/rods, masses.
learnerActions: On a lever diagram, label the load (object being lifted), the effort (force you apply) and the pivot/fulcrum (fixed point it turns on) — learn 'pivot' and 'fulcrum' as the same thing.
Sort everyday objects into lever, pulley or gear: seesaw, crowbar, scissors, wheelbarrow, bottle opener, tweezers, the elbow joint, egg-whisk, flagpole pulley.
For each lever example, mark where the effort, load and pivot are — including trickier arrangements like the wheelbarrow and tweezers.

Match each mechanism to what it changes: a lever reduces the effort when the effort is further from the pivot than the load is (e.g. crowbar, bottle opener, wheelbarrow), but some levers, such as tweezers and the elbow, need a larger effort in exchange for a bigger, faster or more precise movement at the load; a pulley changes direction and (with an extra movable wheel) reduces effort; gears change the size and/or direction of the turning force and the speed of turning.
Answer prediction prompts such as: 'Move the pivot toward the load — does the effort go up or down?'
activities.intendedInsight: Grounding the abstraction in familiar objects, and correctly locating effort/load/pivot even in awkward arrangements, consolidates the vocabulary and challenges over-narrow images (gears only in bikes/cars; pulleys only fixed overhead).

activities.title: Build-and-test extension: gear trains and a block-and-tackle
feedback: If a gear train won't turn, check the cogs mesh; link the small-fast/large-slow behaviour back to what they saw in gear mode.
If adding a movable pulley doesn't seem to help, count the supporting ropes and relate more ropes to lower effort but a greater length of rope to pull.
activities.rationale: Mechanisms are physical, and a hands-on build sandbox is offered as a richer extension where 3D assembly and space matter; the core effort-versus-pivot relationship is already captured in a 2D cross-section, so this enriches rather than replaces the core teaching.
sourceClaims: A lever allows a smaller force to have a greater effect; load = object lifted, effort = force applied, pivot/fulcrum = fixed turning point; effort needed depends on where the pivot sits; gears change size/direction of force (small gear fast/less force, large gear slow/more force); misconception 'all levers work the same way'; equipment = force meters, rulers/rods, masses.
learnerActions: Assemble a simple gear train with different-sized cogs and turn the driver; observe which gear turns faster and which turns with more force.
Rig a real pulley with a string and hanging load, then add a movable wheel to build a simple block-and-tackle; feel the effort change and note any change in pull direction.
Describe how the physical assembly (spacing, meshing, number of supporting ropes) affects what the mechanism does.
activities.intendedInsight: Physically assembling mechanisms adds tangibility and an engineering feel, letting children see how real spacing and meshing produce the force/direction/speed changes modelled elsewhere.

constraints: Keep to the qualitative big idea at this age; reserve the quantitative moment = force × distance (and formal mechanical advantage) for KS3.

Always include the force-for-distance trade so the big idea does not become 'magic': a machine does not create force from nothing — applying a smaller force means moving the effort end a greater distance.

Labelling, sorting and prediction prompts (the classify/label activity) can check and reinforce vocabulary and classification but do not themselves produce the measured relationship or elicit the felt effort drop.

The on-screen workbench models the relationship; a real kit with force meters, rulers/rods, masses and a movable pivot should accompany it so children feel the effort reduction and read a real (noisy) measurement.

Teach 'pivot' and 'fulcrum' as the same fixed turning point; cover all three mechanisms (lever, pulley, gears) and what each changes — and distinguish a fixed pulley (changes direction only) from a movable pulley (reduces effort), and gears beyond bikes/cars.
A static reference image can name parts and show examples but cannot, on its own, display effort falling as the pivot moves; use it as a companion, not the primary teacher of the causal idea.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row's claim that 'a static picture can only assert' the relationship and that a sim is what makes it 'felt' overstates comparative necessity; softened here to scoped affordances and limits. No source establishes comparative efficacy of interactive vs static media.

The 'conversation' artefact was rated a poor fit with the claim that dialogue cannot advance this concept; that universal claim is not supported by the sources and has been omitted rather than propagated.
One source (TeachEngineering — 'Levers That Lift') is marked verified:false in the row; its force-for-distance and fulcrum-position claims are curriculum-consistent but carry lower verification.

Physics check: pushing further from the pivot lets a small effort move a big load; moving the pivot toward the load reduces effort; the smaller applied force is paid for by the effort end moving a greater distance. A single fixed pulley changes direction only, while a movable pulley reduces effort — this distinction is preserved. Small-gear-fast/low-force and large-gear-slow/high-force are retained as stated in the sources.

Activity 1's predict step was realigned so the learner predicts the effect of the variable actually measured (pivot position/effort placement), matching the source's 'predict where to put the pivot' design and the subsequent measurement.

Any specific magnitude of the force-meter drop (and the earlier 'needle halves' detail for one added pulley wheel) is an in-sim illustration, not a guaranteed real-world outcome; wording now says effort 'falls' rather than a fixed ratio.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a ruler-lever on a pencil pivot and a heavy object. Ask them to predict whether it's easier to lift by pushing near the object or far from the pivot, and WHY, before trying both. Predicting 'it makes no difference' or 'it lifts for free' reveals the everyday view; feeling the far push lift it easily — while their hand travels much further — makes the force-distance trade concrete.
probeDeeper: If you move the log (pivot) closer to the rock, is it easier or harder to lift? Why?
Name the load, the effort and the pivot on your bar.
A single pulley on a flagpole — does it make the flag lighter to pull, or just change the direction you pull?
You lifted the rock easily, but what did your end of the bar have to do that the rock didn't?
assess.correctAnswer: It's a lever: the log is the pivot (fulcrum), the rock is the load, the child's push is the effort. Pushing far from the pivot lets a small effort move a big load — a smaller force has a greater effect. It isn't free: the child's end moves a LONGER way (and pushes down further) than the rock rises — the machine trades distance for force, it doesn't create energy.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'The machine gives you the extra force for free — you get more out than you put in.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show the effort end travels much further than the load rises — force is multiplied, distance is traded; nothing is free.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — the lever gives you the lifting force for nothing.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies any cost and can't say what is traded.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'All levers work the same way — the pivot position doesn't matter.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Move the log closer to and further from the rock and feel the effort change; effort depends on where the pivot is.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Thinks moving the fulcrum makes no difference to the effort needed.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Gears and pulleys are only in bikes and cars, and a pulley always hangs from a ceiling.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show varied examples (egg-whisk gears, a flagpole pulley, a movable pulley); a pulley can change the direction of a force and, if movable, reduce the effort.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Can't recognise gears/pulleys in other machines, or assumes only a fixed overhead pulley.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks the machine makes you stronger / lifts for free, or that all levers and pulleys are the same and the pivot doesn't matter.
responseLevels.full: Explains that these mechanisms let a smaller force have a greater effect by applying it further from the pivot (or via extra pulley ropes / different gear sizes), names load/effort/pivot, and recognises the force-for-distance trade — transferring to varied real machines.
responseLevels.partial: Knows a lever/pulley/gear can make a job easier and can name some parts, but explains it as 'gives more force' without the distance trade, or over-generalises one example — stating the effect without the 'nothing for free' idea.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child can't lift a heavy rock by hand, but by pushing down on the far end of a long strong bar resting on a small log, they lift it easily. How does the bar let them lift something they couldn't lift on their own — and are they getting the lift for free?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands says the lever lets a small force do a big job because the effort is applied far from the pivot, AND recognises the trade (their end moves further). A child with the everyday view thinks the bar 'makes them stronger' or gives the lift 'for free', with no sense of the distance trade, or thinks it only works because the bar is special. Tier 2 ('for free?') is the discriminator.
